title: Shithead in 3 minutes
sub: Shithead is a classic and without doubt the most popular card game in hostels around the world. Read it once, play one round, done.
goal: The goal is simple: Get rid of all your cards before the others do. The last player still holding cards loses and is crowned the “Shithead”.
setupLead: You play with a standard 52-card deck, without jokers. The game is easy to learn, but its mix of luck and tactics gives it surprising depth.
dealP: Everyone gets 9 cards in three layers.
setupAlt: In front of each player are three piles, each with one face-down and one face-up card, plus three cards in hand.
lgHand: 3 in your handonly you see them
setupP: Do not look at your face-down cards. The rest of the deck goes in the middle as the draw pile.
swLead: Before the game starts, you can swap any cards between your hand and your face-up cards. This is your only chance to prepare your table – choose wisely!
swAlt: The face-up 4 on the table is swapped with the ace from the hand.
w1p: Look at your 3 hand cards and your 3 face-up cards. The face-down ones stay face-down.
w2p: Swap as many cards between your hand and your face-up cards as you like.
w3p: In the end you have 3 face-up cards in front of you and 3 in your hand. Once everyone is done, the game starts.
swWhy: You only play your face-up cards at the very end, without a hand to fall back on. So put strong cards face-up: high cards like aces and kings, or special cards like the 2, 3 and 10. You can play cards of the same rank together. You’ll learn what the special cards do further down under special cards.
rankLead: The 2 is the lowest card, the ace the highest. Suits (♠♥♦♣) don’t matter.
rankAlt: Card order from low to high: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, Jack, Queen, King, Ace.
rankP: J = Jack, Q = Queen, K = King, A = Ace.
turnLead: Look at the top card of the discard pile. Then there’s only one question:
dq: Do you have a card that’s equal or higher?
dqs: You can always play a 2, 3 or 10 – more on that under special cards.
by1: Play it face-up on the discard pile. You can play several cards of the same rank together, for example three 6s.
by2: Draw until you have 3 cards in your hand again, as long as the draw pile still has cards. If you still have 3 or more, you don’t draw.
bn1: Pick up the whole discard pile into your hand.
dnext: Either way, it’s then the next player’s turn, clockwise.
startP: Whoever has a 4 in their hand plays it and starts. If nobody has a 4, the next higher card starts, so a 5 and so on. After that, play goes clockwise.
spLead: These cards have a special effect. You can always play the 2, 3 and 10, no matter what’s on top.
sp2p: Resets the value of the pile – the next player can play any card. Can be played on any card.
sp3p: It mirrors the value of the card played before it. So the next player has to beat the card under the 3. Can be played on any card.
sp7p: The next player has to play a card of the same or a lower value (instead of a higher one).
sp8p: The next player misses a turn.
sp10p: The most powerful card in the deck. The whole pile is removed from the game. You get to play again right away. Can be played on any card.
sp4p: If four cards of the same rank are on top (even from different players), the pile burns automatically.
e1p: Then nobody draws anymore. You keep playing as usual, but your hand gets smaller with every turn. If you have to pick up the discard pile, you get more cards again, of course.
e2p: Only once the draw pile is gone and you have no cards left in your hand do you play from the table: first your face-up cards, then the face-down ones.
e3p: You play a face-up card just like one from your hand, and several of the same rank together. If you can’t play any, you pick up the discard pile and first play your hand empty again.
e4p: Turn one card over and put it on the pile (you have to show it). If it fits, great. If not, you pick it up together with the discard pile and first play those empty again.
e5p: Once you’re out of cards, you’ve won. The last one at the table is the Shithead and deals the next round.
qLead: Quick test. One card is on top, you have one in your hand.
foot: Have fun at the table. And remember: you’re only the Shithead if you can’t laugh about it.
nfP: Maybe someone played a 10 and burned it. Or it’s already out, like everyone who has no cards left. Except you.
nfBtn: Pick up the pile and read the rules

strategy.sub: The ultimate Shithead strategy guide. The game is easy to learn, but its mix of luck and strategy gives it surprising depth.
strategy.principle: Shithead isn’t about winning. It’s about not losing. Play tactically for yourself, because in the end you only want one thing: not to be the Shithead.
strategy.swapLead: The card swap at the start is one of the most important strategic decisions. All the other players see your face-up cards, and they’re locked in. So choose wisely.
up: The 10 – always. If you have a 10 before the start, put it down as a face-up card. Play it as the last of your face-up cards. Thanks to the burn you go again right away and can immediately play a face-down card.
Several 10s: Don’t necessarily put both face-up. Played together they are one single move instead of several. Better keep one in your hand as a backup.
Special cards: Any card with an ability is good. The invisible 3 and the 10 are the strongest in the late game. The 2 is good too, but the next player can play anything after it.
High cards (K, Q, J): They’re easy to play, because only a few cards beat them.

Pairs: You play two matching face-up cards at the same time. If there’s a 10 next to them, take two low matching cards rather than two different high ones. With the 10 behind them, the low value doesn’t matter.
strategy.notUp: What doesn’t go on top: low cards like 4, 5 and 6. In the endgame you can hardly play them, and then you have to play them without any hand cards.
strategy.exAlt: Example swap. Dealt: face-up 4, 8 and queen, in hand 10, 5 and king. After the swap: face-up 10, king and queen, in hand 4, 5 and 8.
strategy.exWhy: Why? You get rid of the low cards early, while there are still cards to draw. Only strong cards lie on top, and in the end the 10 gives you a direct path to your face-down cards.
strategy.exVariant: Variant: face-up 10 · 6 · 6. The pair plus the 10 saves moves.

items: Picking up early is okay. A small pile at the start hardly hurts and sometimes brings good cards. A big pile of low cards at the end is the real problem.

Bad starting hand: Try to draw as quickly as possible, or pick up the pile. If it only has 3–4 cards and they improve your hand, picking up is often better than wasting a special card. Try to break the flow of the game while your opponent is drawing by picking up the pile.
Don’t play high cards at the same time while there are still cards to draw. The chance that better cards will come is low.
Hoard special cards. 2, 3 and 10 are worth much more in the late game, so don’t waste them early.
Keep an eye on the pile. If two matching cards are already on top, you might be able to complete a Four of a Kind Burn.
Get rid of low cards. Play 4, 5, 6 and 9 as quickly as possible. Keeping a 7 in your hand can make tactical sense. If your opponent only has high cards left, they have to pick up.
Think of your face-up cards. If you have a low (face-up) card you can’t play, play a 2 and hope the others also only play low cards.
Count cards. Remember which special cards have already been played. If all the 10s are gone, the pile can only be burned with a Four of a Kind Burn.
Weak face-up cards first. When you control the pile, you get rid of your worst face-up cards early.
Combine hand cards with face-up cards. At the end you can play your last hand cards together with matching face-up cards, for example to finish a Four of a Kind Burn.
Take high cards out of the game. If you have very bad face-up cards, even a burn with four 2s or four 3s on high cards can make sense, so the high cards are gone. Otherwise you’d better not play it.
Pick up voluntarily. Before you play a good card like the 10 and then can’t get rid of your face-up or face-down cards, rather pick up a pile with good cards.

Watch your opponents. If several players are still in the game and one of them only has 1–2 cards left, they’ll be out very quickly anyway. Still play for yourself first, even if that lets them go out: better one player fewer, while you keep your high cards and probably won’t be the Shithead. Focus on the other players.

Reset and picking up open up the game. After a 2 (and likewise after a 4, the lowest normal card) the next player can play any card, including any face-down card. The same applies when you have to pick up.
Face-down cards are pure luck. There’s no strategy here, only hope – although some say it’s skill 😉

strategy.spLead: Each ability changes the game in its own way. Whoever masters the timing stands out from the others and won’t be the Shithead.

sp.p: Can always be played, but it’s the lowest card, and the next player can play anything after it. Save it for moments when the pile is too high.

Seriously underrated. With it you can pass on a pile with high cards. There’s a real chance your opponent has a higher card like a queen or king, so play other cards first before you play the 3. It’s also your safety net against a 7.
The next player has to play a card of the same or lower value. The 7 can be played incredibly tactically. Whoever masters it often decides who becomes the Shithead.

Gets stronger the fewer players are left. Skip the player who’s about to go out, or someone who’s playing well right now. Several 8s skip several players. You can also skip so that it’s your turn again right away, and then play a lower card like the 9, for example. But that only works if the order fits.
The strongest card. It burns the pile and you go again.
items: Rather try to play the card last, as a backup, and don’t burn a big pile early. That way your opponent has to pick up a big pile.
After you’ve burned, put down your lowest card.
Because you go again after the burn, later on you can get rid of your (low) face-up and face-down cards very well.

sp.p: Four matching cards in a row burn the pile. If you’ve counted or know that all four cards are in your hand, don’t play them all, but rather try to burn with the last card – that’s how you complete the Four of a Kind Burn on purpose.

mistakes: Ignoring your opponents’ face-up cards. If they all only have low cards face-up, keep the pile high and force them to pick up. Especially with the 7 you can play tactically here. If an opponent has a king face-up, for example, you know your Four of a Kind Burn with kings won’t work right now.
Not counting. Once all four 2s have been played, nobody can reset anymore, and that changes the whole game. Also remember which cards your opponents pick up from the pile. Especially special cards!
Putting low cards face-up. 4s, 5s and 6s are hard to play in the endgame.
Giving away special cards. A 2, 3 or 10 is your emergency exit. Don’t give it away if you can play normally.
Splitting up pairs. Playing matching cards together saves moves, and with the fourth matching card you burn the pile.

Playing matching cards wrong. You have two kings, your opponent one and nobody has anything higher: if you play both at once, they play their king and you have to pick up. If you play them one at a time (you K, them K, you K), they have to pick up.

info.cardsAlt: 52 cards from ace to king, without jokers
info.intro: Shithead is easy to learn and fun at any age. It takes a bit of skill, but to win you also need some luck. With these simple rules you’ll learn Shithead in a few minutes.

quick.rule: Play cards whose value is equal to or higher than the pile. If you can’t, pick up the pile.
quick.sp4: Four of the same in a row burn the pile
quick.sp4extra: You can “throw in” cards of the same rank at any time to complete it – even when it isn’t actually your turn. Whoever completes the burn gets to play on right away.
quick.tryH: Still unsure? Try it right now!

rules.bnFree: You can also do this voluntarily, even if you had a card that fits.
rules.varLead: Shithead is extremely flexible and adapts to any group size:
rules.var1: 4 players: This is the ideal number of players for the best dynamics, strategy and the right amount of luck.
rules.var2: 6 players: Here you play with only two face-down/face-up cards instead of three, so the deck is enough.
rules.var3: 7+ players: Time for a second deck! The rules stay the same, and the “four of a kind” rule still applies across both decks.
rules.faq1q: Can I play several cards at once?
rules.faq1a: Yes! If you have two, three or even four cards of the same rank (e.g. three queens), you can play them all in one turn. This is great for completing a Four of a Kind Burn.
rules.faq2q: What happens when I pick up the pile?
rules.faq2a: All the cards go into your hand and your turn ends. It’s the next player’s turn, and they can play any card.
rules.faq3q: Can I pick up the pile even if I could play?
rules.faq3a: Yes, by default! It can be a clever tactical move – for example, if the pile is small and contains lots of useful cards (like aces or special cards), it can be worth picking it up to be better prepared for the endgame.
rules.faq4q: Can I swap my face-up cards?
rules.faq4a: Yes! Before the game starts, you can swap your three face-up cards with your hand cards as you like. Your strongest cards should lie face-up on the table.
rules.faq5q: Can I look at my face-down cards?
rules.faq5a: No! Face-down cards stay unknown until you play them. You have to show them, even if you have to pick up the pile. This keeps the game exciting and unpredictable right to the end.
rules.faq6q: When one player has no cards left, does the game go on?
rules.faq6a: Yes! It’s not about winning, it’s about not losing. Don’t be the shithead!
rules.faq7q: How long does a game take?
rules.faq7a: Most games take about 10 to 15 minutes. New players usually understand how it works after just one round.
rules.faq8q: What other names does the game go by?
rules.faq8a: Shithead has lots of names. The most common are Palace, Karma and Shed; you may also hear China Hand, Ten-Two Slide or Zweeds pesten. The basic idea is the same everywhere, only the house rules differ – see Variants.
